title: Intercontinental de Aviación 256
summary: Intercontinental de Aviación Flight 256, a 29-year-old Douglas DC-9-14, crashed into a marshy lagoon near María La Baja during approach to Cartagena. The aircraft descended below safe altitude and impacted terrain 56 km from the airport. Investigation determined the probable cause was incorrect altimeter setting, with altitude number 1 indicating 16200 ft on impact. Altitude number 2's lights did not work, preventing crew comparison and detection of the error. Contributing factors included lack of radar observation and insufficient training.
probable_cause: Wrong setting of the altimeter, resulting in altitude misjudgment and controlled flight into terrain. Contributing factors included lack of radar observation and crew loss of situational awareness during clear weather.

title: 1995 Antonov An-70 prototype crash
summary: The first Antonov An-70 prototype collided with an Antonov An-72 support aircraft at 16:09 CET over Borodianka Raion in Ukraine. All seven crew members on the An-70 were killed; the An-72 landed safely with no fatalities. A Ukrainian commission blamed careless formation flying and human error by both crews, noting that previous test flights had revealed flight control problems.
probable_cause: Human error and careless actions of both crews in their formation flying led to collision and crash.

title: TAROM 371
summary: A TAROM Airbus A310 took off with the First Officer as pilot flying. The autothrottle reduced the left engine to idle, creating asymmetric thrust. The captain became incapacitated, and the First Officer, unfamiliar with Western-style attitude indicators and distracted by the captain's condition, failed to recognize the aircraft's severe left bank. The aircraft crashed near Balotești just 89 seconds after takeoff, killing all 60 people on board.
probable_cause: The autothrottle malfunction reduced the left engine to idle during climb. The captain became incapacitated, and the First Officer's confusion between Western and Soviet attitude indicator designs, combined with failure to recognize the deteriorating situation, led to loss of control.

title: Knight Air 816
summary: Knight Air Flight 816, an Embraer 110 Bandeirante, crashed shortly after takeoff from Leeds Bradford Airport in poor weather with restricted visibility and recent thunderstorm activity. One minute and 50 seconds into the flight, the crew reported problems with the artificial horizons and requested to return to the airport. While maneuvering to return, the aircraft entered a left turn, rapidly lost height and crashed at Dunkeswick Moor. The AAIB found that one or both artificial horizons failed, leading to loss of control and a spiral dive exceeding operating parameters before partial breakup on impact.
probable_cause: One or both artificial horizon instruments failed, causing the pilots to lose control and enter a spiral dive that broke up the aircraft before impact.

title: Ansett New Zealand 703
summary: During a non-precision VOR/DME instrument approach to runway 25 at Palmerston North in 5 km visibility, the right main landing gear failed to extend. The captain ordered the first officer to perform the alternate gear extension procedure. Distracted by the first officer's attempts to lower the gear, the captain allowed the aircraft to drift off-profile from the 14 nmi DME arc toward the rising terrain of the Tararua Range. The GPWS warning sounded with insufficient time to avert impact. The aircraft struck high ground twice before final impact, breaking apart with the landing gear still retracted.
probable_cause: Captain distraction during alternate landing gear extension procedure resulted in loss of approach profile adherence and terrain impact in low visibility conditions; GPWS warning provided insufficient warning time.

title: Aviateca 901
summary: An Aviateca Boeing 737 on approach to El Salvador deviated from the standard approach due to heavy rain and thunderstorms. The crew intercepted the wrong ILS glide slope without briefing ATC of the deviation. ATC, unaware of the aircraft's true position, cleared a descent. The ground proximity warning system activated but too late. The aircraft crashed into the San Vicente volcano at 7,159 feet, killing all 65 on board.
probable_cause: The flight crew's lack of situational awareness in relation to the 7,159 foot San Vicente volcano obstruction and its decision to descend, combined with ineffective crew resource management.

title: Atlantic Southeast Airlines 529
summary: Atlantic Southeast Airlines Flight 529, an Embraer EMB 120 Brasilia, crashed on August 21, 1995, while climbing through 18,100 feet between Atlanta and Gulfport. The outboard section of one Hamilton Standard propeller blade on the left engine separated, imbalancing the propeller and causing the entire assembly to become dislodged from violent wobbling. The separation distorted the engine nacelle and wing profile, causing excessive drag and loss of lift on the left wing. The aircraft rapidly lost altitude and the crew diverted to a field near Carrollton, Georgia. Before emergency landing could commence, the aircraft pitched over into an uncommanded dive, struck trees, and crashed nose-first.
probable_cause: Propeller blade failure due to undiscovered metal fatigue in one blade resulting from corrosion from chlorine. The blade, which had been rejected during ultrasonic testing and sent for refurbishing, was incorrectly repaired by Hamilton Standard and then installed on the propeller fitted to the aircraft on September 30, 1994. Hamilton Standard and the FAA failed to require recurrent on-wing ultrasonic inspections.

events.text: Flight 529 took off from Atlanta at 12:23 Eastern Daylight Time and climbed normally.

The flight crew initially tried to return to Atlanta for an emergency landing but the rapid descent resulted in them being diverted to West Georgia Regional Airport.
The airplane was unable to stay in the air long enough and the pilots began searching for an open space to make an emergency landing in a field near Carrollton.
Before the emergency landing could commence, the aircraft pitched over and began an uncommanded dive, striking the tops of the trees before hitting the ground nose first.

title: Malaysia Airlines 2133
summary: The Fokker 50 descended too steeply and fast on approach to Tawau due to a late descent clearance. Despite warnings from the first officer about excessive speed, the captain maintained high speed. The aircraft touched down 3400 feet down the runway, bounced, and landed again at 4800 feet, leaving only 800 feet to stop. The aircraft overran the runway and crashed into a shanty town.
probable_cause: Captain's decision to continue approach with excessive speed and steep descent rate despite warnings, combined with late descent clearance, resulting in long landing and runway overrun. Airline fuel-saving and punctuality policies influenced the captain's decision to land despite insufficient stopping distance.

title: Air-military parade accident on September 16, 1995 (Mexico)
summary: During a military parade celebrating Mexican independence, a Northrop F-5E collided with a Lockheed T-33 in a chain reaction midair collision involving five aircraft total. The F-5E piloted by Captain Héctor Ricardo Trejo Flores struck the lead T-33 (JE-050), triggering collisions with three additional T-33s (JE-036, JE-009, JE-049). Six of nine pilots were killed; survivors included pilots of JE-009 who landed safely and two from JE-036 who ejected.
probable_cause: Multiple factors including T-33 route invasion at incorrect altitude, aircraft flying above assigned altitude, and desynchronization during formation maneuvers.

title: 1995 Alaska Boeing E-3 Sentry accident
summary: A United States Air Force Boeing E-3 Sentry ingested a flock of Canada geese into engines 1 and 2 during departure from Elmendorf Air Force Base. With the loss of thrust from both left engines and a full fuel load, the aircraft was unable to maintain altitude. The E-3 crashed into a wooded area less than one mile from the runway end only 42 seconds after takeoff, killing all 24 crew members.

title: Nigeria Airways 357
summary: Flight 357 on approach to Kaduna requested and was allowed to land on runway 23 despite air traffic control warning of tailwind conditions. The aircraft descended in an unstable approach with a steep left turn misaligning it with runway centerline. The aircraft touched down 615 meters from runway end after overrunning 79.5% of the runway length, deployed thrust reversers but entered an uncontrollable skid. The right wing struck the ground, ruptured fuel tanks, and caused fire and explosion. 11 passengers were killed.
probable_cause: Unstable approach with misalignment resulted in long landing on runway with tailwind, causing runway overrun and subsequent structural damage and fire.

title: Cameroon Airlines 3701
summary: On 3 December 1995, Cameroon Airlines Flight 3701 was on a second approach to Douala when the No. 1 engine lost power due to structural fatigue in a first-stage compressor blade. During the go-around attempt with one engine failed, the pilots did not notice the degraded performance, and the aircraft entered a steep dive before crashing in a mangrove swamp. The investigation determined that late execution of the go-around procedure with unidentified single-engine configuration led to irreversible loss of speed and loss of control.
probable_cause: Loss of control during a go-around attempt with degraded performance. Contributing factors: detachment by structural fatigue of the No. 1 engine first-stage compressor blade and late execution of the go-around procedure in single-engine configuration.

title: Azerbaijan Airlines 56
summary: At 60 m altitude with airspeed of 317 km/h, the No. 1 engine failed. The co-pilot initially countered the left bank, but the flight engineer reported in error that the No. 2 engine had failed. The captain ordered the No. 2 (operating) engine shut down. Unable to maintain altitude on no engines, the aircraft descended into an apartment block area where it crashed with a 37-degree right bank.
probable_cause: The No. 1 engine failed due to vibration that loosened and displaced engine mount nuts, causing engine turbines to shift and become damaged. The No. 2 operating engine was shut down in error based on the flight engineer's erroneous report.

The flight engineer reported, in error, that the no. 2 engine had failed; the captain then ordered the no. 2 engine to be shut down; the no. 2 engine had already stopped.
The aircraft climbed to an altitude of 197 m while the speed had decreased to 290 km/h; the aircraft then crashed into a field with a 37-degree right bank and a sink rate of 10 m/s.

title: Khabarovsk United Air Group 3949
summary: Khabarovsk United Air Group Flight 3949 crashed on 7 December 1995 during automated flight at 10600 m, killing all ninety-eight people aboard. The aircraft had instantaneously banked to the left shortly after taking off due to mechanical failure. Following maintenance, the aircraft had a tendency to roll to the left without any command from the pilots, but this issue was not rectified. The crew were unaware that the aircraft had banked to the right. Without proper monitoring and lack of alarm, the aircraft entered a heavy turn to the right, spiralling down without any possible recovery.
probable_cause: The crash was caused by a combination of mechanical failure, pilot error and design flaw. An unresolved mechanical issue causing roll to the left led the crew to conduct fuel transfer as a corrective action. The crew were unaware the aircraft had banked to the right, and without adequate monitoring systems or warnings, the aircraft entered an unrecoverable spiral descent.

title: Banat Air 166
summary: Banat Air Flight 166, an Antonov An-24, crashed shortly after takeoff from Verona-Villafranca Airport on 13 December 1995 with eight crew and 41 passengers aboard. The aircraft was severely overloaded by about 2000 kilograms and its wings were contaminated with ice and snow because the pilot declined to have it deiced. Shortly after liftoff the airspeed dropped dramatically, and despite nose-down then nose-up control inputs the aircraft entered a steep bank at 67 degrees and struck the ground.
probable_cause: The accident resulted from multiple factors: disruption of airflow over wings due to ice formation from taking off without deicing, severe overloading, and spatial disorientation of the crew during emergency control inputs.

factors.evidence: The aircraft's wings were contaminated with ice and snow; the pilot declined to have the plane deiced.

title: American Airlines 965
summary: During approach to Cali, the crew opted for a straight-in approach and mistakenly cleared all programmed approach waypoints from the FMS. The pilots selected the wrong radiobeacon identifier (R instead of ROZO), causing the autopilot to fly toward Bogotá. The aircraft descended into a valley north of Cali with ground proximity warning activated 12 seconds before impact. The crew attempted to climb clear, but fully extended speed brakes prevented adequate rate of climb, leading to stick shaker activation and terrain impact at 8,920 feet.
probable_cause: Navigational errors by the flight crew, specifically the selection of the wrong radiobeacon identifier and the failure to retract speed brakes during the escape maneuver.
